:::{.def}

While last section uses synthetic data, projects usually require real data.

In this section, we look at three ways to obtain data: [Torchvision built-in datasets](https://pytorch.org/vision/stable/datasets.html), [Hugging Face Hub](https://huggingface.co/datasets), and your own data read with a custom class.

:::

## Our working dataset: EuroSAT

Throughout this course we will use a single task: classifying satellite images by land use. [EuroSAT](https://github.com/phelber/eurosat) is a set of 27,000 small (64 × 64 pixels) RGB patches from [Sentinel-2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sentinel-2) images, each labelled with one of 10 land-use classes.

It is a good fit for us: real research data (remote sensing), yet small enough (~90 MiB) to download and train on quickly, even on modest GPUs. It is distributed under an MIT licence (credit: [Helber et al. 2019](https://doi.org/10.1109/JSTARS.2019.2918242)).

## Packages

```{python}
from collections import Counter
from pathlib import Path

import datasets as hf
import torch
from matplotlib import pyplot as plt
from PIL import Image
from torch.utils.data import Dataset, random_split
from torchvision.datasets import EuroSAT
```

- `torch.utils.data` holds the dataset machinery: the [`Dataset`](https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/data.html) base class and `random_split`.
- `torchvision.datasets` provides ready-made vision datasets, `EuroSAT` among them.
- `datasets` is the Hugging Face data library.
- `PIL.Image` opens image files and `Counter` will tally labels.

## Torchvision datasets

```{python}
eurosat = EuroSAT(root="data", download=True)
print(len(eurosat), "images")
print(eurosat.classes)
```

`download=True` fetches and extracts the archive into `data/` on the first run, then detects the files and skips the download. On disk, this is the classic layout, one folder per class:

[data/eurosat/2750/AnnualCrop/AnnualCrop_1.jpg]{.codelike}
[data/eurosat/2750/Forest/Forest_1.jpg]{.codelike}
...

:::{.note}

Dataset classes holding data for PyTorch must implement the functions `__init__` (instantiates the class), `__len__` (returns the number of samples in the dataset) and `__getitem__` (returns one sample at a time).

:::

```{python}
img, label = eurosat[0]
print(type(img).__name__, img.size, img.mode)
print(label, eurosat.classes[label])
```

- Images are not read when the dataset is created: initialization only scans file names, and indexing decodes that one image.
- We get a PIL image, not a tensor: converting images to tensors happens in preprocessing (a later page covers transforms).
- The label is the index of the class in `eurosat.classes` (alphabetical, so the numbering is stable).

Let's display one image for each class:

```{python}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 5, figsize=(12, 5))
for ax, cls in zip(axes.flat, range(len(eurosat.classes))):
    img, _ = eurosat[eurosat.targets.index(cls)]
    ax.imshow(img)
    ax.set_title(eurosat.classes[cls], fontsize=9)
    ax.axis("off")
```

### Class balance

Never trust a dataset to be balanced. `eurosat.targets` holds the labels:

```{python}
counts = Counter(eurosat.targets)
for i, name in enumerate(eurosat.classes):
    print(f"{name:>22} {counts[i]}")
```

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
ax.barh(eurosat.classes, [counts[c] for c in range(10)])
ax.set_xlabel("number of images")
```

EuroSAT has 2,000 to 3,000 images per class: a mild imbalance. When classes are heavily skewed, a high accuracy can hide a model that ignores the rare classes entirely; we will come back to this when evaluating models.

### Train and validation sets

**Never evaluate a model on data it learned from.**

We split EuroSAT, 80% for training and 20% for validation:

```{python}
train, val = random_split(
    eurosat, [0.8, 0.2], generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(42)
)
print(len(train), len(val), type(train).__name__)
```

- `random_split` returns two `Subset` objects: thin views holding lists of indices into `eurosat`. No image is copied.
- The seeded generator makes the shuffle reproducible.
- `Subset`s satisfy the Dataset contract too: they can be indexed, or wrapped in DataLoaders (next page).

:::{.note}

`random_split` does not respect class balance. With EuroSAT's mild imbalance this hardly matters, but on small or heavily skewed data, draw a stratified split yourself (same class proportions in both parts).

:::

:::{.exo}

:::{.yourturn}

Your turn:

:::

:::

The rest of the course must evaluate on this exact validation set, or numbers from different pages would not be comparable. So we save the index lists once:

```{python}
torch.save({"train": train.indices, "val": val.indices}, "data/split.pt")
```

Later pages reload them with:

```{.python}
idx = torch.load("data/split.pt", weights_only=True)
train = torch.utils.data.Subset(eurosat, idx["train"])
```

## Hugging Face Hub

The [Hub](https://huggingface.co/datasets) mirrors thousands of datasets and researchers increasingly share their data there. The [datasets library](https://huggingface.co/docs/datasets/quickstart) downloads and caches them, carries metadata along, preprocesses in parallel, and streams datasets too big to fit on disk.

```{python}
eurosat_hf = hf.load_dataset("blanchon/EuroSAT_RGB")
train_hf = eurosat_hf["train"]
print(train_hf)
```

The first call downloads the data into `~/.cache/huggingface`; later calls hit the cache and return instantly. We get a `DatasetDict` of named splits: this copy of EuroSAT comes pre-split into train/validation/test.

```{python}
label_meta = train_hf.features["label"]
print(label_meta.names)
```

The labels come documented with the data: the `label` column is a `ClassLabel` feature that knows the class names.

```{python}
print(train_hf[0]["label"], train_hf[0]["filename"])
```

Indexing an HF dataset returns a dict, not a tuple: columns have names instead of positions.

`.map` applies a function to every example, in parallel (`num_proc=`), and caches the result on disk, keyed by a fingerprint of the function. Try running this next cell twice:

```{python}
def add_label_name(example):
    return {"label_name": label_meta.int2str(example["label"])}

train_hf = train_hf.map(add_label_name)
print(train_hf[0]["label_name"])
```

With `streaming=True`, examples arrive shard by shard as they download. There is no `len()` and no random access: a way to peek into a dataset without storing it.

```{python}
stream = hf.load_dataset("blanchon/EuroSAT_RGB", split="train", streaming=True)
first = next(iter(stream))
print(first["filename"])
```

:::{.note}

HF datasets satisfy the same `__len__`/`__getitem__` contract (with dict examples), so they plug into the same DataLoaders as everything else; `with_format("torch")` returns the labels as tensors.

:::

## Custom Dataset

The most common situation of all: a folder of images on your machine, arranged somehow, that you need to train on. If they sit in one folder per class (exactly the layout EuroSAT uses on disk), a dozen lines give you a Dataset:

```{python}
class ImageFiles(Dataset):
    """Images in one subfolder per class under root; labels from folder names."""

    def __init__(self, root, transform=None, extensions=(".jpg", ".jpeg", ".png")):
        root = Path(root)
        # sorted: alphabetical class names give deterministic, portable
        # label indices (the same convention as ImageFolder)
        self.classes = sorted(p.name for p in root.iterdir() if p.is_dir())
        self.class_to_idx = {name: i for i, name in enumerate(self.classes)}
        self.transform = transform
        # scan the file list once (paths only: no image is read yet);
        # walking class by class gives ImageFolder's order
        self.samples = [
            (path, label)
            for label, name in enumerate(self.classes)
            for path in sorted((root / name).iterdir())
            if path.suffix.lower() in extensions
        ]

    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.samples)

    def __getitem__(self, index):
        path, label = self.samples[index]
        # convert("RGB"): one stray grayscale or RGBA file should not
        # crash a training run
        img = Image.open(path).convert("RGB")
        if self.transform is not None:  # used on the preprocessing page
            img = self.transform(img)
        return img, label
```

- `__init__` scans the tree once and stores `(path, label)` pairs: paths only, no image is opened. Classes are sorted alphabetically, the same convention as `ImageFolder`, so label numbering matches.
- `__getitem__` opens one image per call: decoding on demand is what will let worker processes parallelize the reading (next page).
- `.convert("RGB")` prevents one stray grayscale or RGBA file from crashing training.
- `transform` is the hook where preprocessing will plug in (a later page).

Let's point it at the EuroSAT tree:

```{python}
eurosat_custom = ImageFiles(Path("data") / "eurosat" / "2750")
img, label = eurosat_custom[0]
print(len(eurosat_custom), "images,", len(eurosat_custom.classes), "classes")
print(type(img).__name__, img.size, "->", label, eurosat_custom.classes[label])
```

### Comparison with Torchvision

```{python}
print(eurosat_custom.classes == eurosat.classes)
```

```{python}
print([lbl for _, lbl in eurosat_custom.samples] == eurosat.targets)
```

Our dataset agrees with Torchvision's reader, class for class and label for label. `torchvision.datasets.ImageFolder` is actually exactly the class we defined. If your data is more messy, you can adapt this class to transform and tidy it. Our section on [data preprocessing](../jxai/jxai_preprocess.qmd) in our [deep learning course with the JAX AI stack](../top_jxai.qmd) goes into this in a lot more details.
